records.text: A single piece now reaches several targets at once. That is the fork.
Something waits on the other side's turn. One of their pieces could attack several targets at once, a fork.
A fork sat inside another move, one piece reaching several targets together. This move leaves it untouched.
The piece on that line cannot leave it. It is pinned to its king, and stepping off would expose the king.
Look along the line to the king. The other side can pin a piece there, and a pinned piece cannot leave without exposing its king.
Another move held a pin to the king. The pinned piece would have been fixed to its line, unable to step off without exposing the king behind it.
Two pieces stand on one line. The attack meets the front one first, and when it steps aside, the piece behind is exposed. A skewer.
The front piece is not alone on its line. The other side can try a skewer, and moving that front piece could expose what stands behind it.
A stronger move had a skewer in it. Had the front piece stepped aside, the one behind it would have been exposed.
The defender is the target. Capture it, and what it protected loses that protection.
One defender is holding something in place. The other side can now capture it, and what it guards could be left without protection.
A different move could have captured a defender. What it guarded would have stood without that protection.
The king is walled in by its own pieces. This move uses that: a back-rank mate pattern.
The king's own pieces stand where it would need to escape. That gives the other side a route to a back-rank mate.
A back-rank mate was available, the king hemmed in by its own pieces. This move goes another way, and the mate goes unplayed.
A pawn has a road to the last rank. When it arrives, it becomes a new piece. That is the aim here.
One of their pawns now has a way toward the last rank. This gives the other side a chance to promote it.
A stronger move opened the way for a pawn to reach the last rank and promote. This move does not take that road.
One piece steps out of the line. Behind it, another piece was already aimed. That is the discovered attack.
One of their pieces is screening another. If it steps aside, the piece behind can attack. This allows that discovered attack.
Another move had a discovered attack: one piece stepping aside to uncover a threat from the piece behind. After this move, that threat stays hidden.
Two threats arrive from one move. That is a double attack, two attacks working together.
Two threats could arrive together now. This gives the other side a double attack, both made with one move.
A stronger move made two attacks at once. That double attack goes unused here.
A defender is drawn away from its post. What it was covering is left open. That is the deflection.
One defender carries an important task. The other side can now draw it away, a deflection, and that task would go uncovered.
Another move could have drawn a defender away from its task. That deflection is not used.
A piece stood with no guard. The idea is simply to take it.
Another move could have taken an undefended piece. Nothing was guarding it, and this move does not take it.
A piece is left behind with no guard. The other side can take it.
Notice what just left. This move takes away a piece's only real defender, and the other side can capture what it left behind.
The threat arrived with the opponent's last move. It is still waiting, unanswered, and a piece can now be captured.
The capture is only the first half. Then the recapture takes a piece of greater value. Count the whole exchange.
A minor piece is off its starting square now. It is in play.
A different move would have developed a minor piece, lifting it from its starting square.
The rook stands on an open file. No pawn of either color is on it.
Another move would have placed a rook on an open file, empty of pawns of either color.
The rook now stands on a semi-open file. None of its own pawns are there, and at least one enemy pawn still is.
With another move, a rook would have stood on a semi-open file, clear of its own pawns, with an enemy pawn still on it.
This pawn has no enemy pawn ahead of it, on its own file or either file beside it. It is passed.
Another move would have made a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or either neighboring file.
The passed pawn moves forward. It was passed before; now it stands nearer the last rank.
Another move would have pushed the passed pawn forward, nearer the last rank.
A pawn stands alone now. No friendly pawn is on either file beside it. It is isolated.
A different move would have left an isolated pawn, with no friendly pawn on either neighboring file.
A piece that stood alone now has a defender.
Another move would have given an undefended piece a defender.
Nothing defends this piece now. That is worth seeing, though it does not mean the piece can be won.
With another move, a piece would have been left with no defender. That alone would not mean it could be won.
A square opens beside the king. It has a legal flight square now that it did not have before.
Another move would have given the king a new legal flight square.
The king steps aside to castle, and the rook crosses over to stand beside it.
Castling was the alternative, moving king and rook together.
This capture breaks a bishop pair. One color of square is now left without that side's bishop.
Another move would have captured a bishop, breaking the other side's bishop pair.
Two pawns of one color now share a file. Doubled pawns.
A different move would have left doubled pawns, two of one color on the same file.
The king's defenses no longer hold. The other side can force checkmate now. Follow the attack in, one move at a time.
A forced checkmate was there. This move leaves it behind. Going back, the finish can still be found.
The offered material can be taken. In the line that was checked, taking it does not refute the sacrifice.
Every other move that was checked was losing. This one alone kept the position playable.
This was the lone keeper of the advantage. The other moves that were checked were losing.
A capture is already waiting in the reply. Something can be taken at once.
The strongest reply is a check. The king has to be answered first.
Another move is the engine's choice. Set it on the board beside this one, and the replies differ.
This move is weaker than the engine's best. The difference shows in the reply.
A strong move. Among those the engine examined, it gives away very little.
A sound move. The engine prefers another, but much of the position's value remains.
A natural move, by the human-move model. The engine finds a stronger one, and the reply is where the difference shows.
The human-move model rarely expects this move. The engine still rates it strong.
One move kept the position playable, and the engine found it. The human-move model sees it slipping past most players. Here it was missed.
This one was hard to find, by the human-move model and the alternatives checked. Keep it for positions like this.
The position held because of this move. The human-move model and the searched alternatives suggest it was a hard defense to see.
Natural, by the human-move model. Best, by the engine. Here they point to the same move.
The human-move model finds this natural. The engine finds it strong, though another move ranks higher.
Very little time remained on the clock before this move.
The clock shows a quick move. Time was still left.
The clock shows a long pause before this move.
This move is in a recognized opening line. The ground is known here.
The recognized line ends here. From this move on, the opening book is silent.
After the earlier setback, the position is playable again. This move brings it back.
Earlier the position slipped; now it can be held again. The other side's errors helped make that possible.
The opponent's last move left an opening. This move takes it.
The opponent's last move left an opportunity. This move leaves it unused.
The same issue has appeared earlier in this game. It returns here, and the earlier moments carry the same warning sign.
The piece left alone before has a guardian once more.
No single move did this. Several small concessions have worn the position down, and this is one of them.
The advantage held through every reviewed move, to the recorded win. That stretch shows how it was kept.
This issue appears in other saved games too. It has been here before, and those games belong beside this one.
Checkmate. The king cannot escape. It is over.
Checkmate. The king has no legal escape left. The earlier defense is where to look now.
The game ends in a draw. Earlier decisions are still there to review.
The board is quiet. Choose your move when you see it.
That attempt does not work. The answer is still on the board.
Nothing came back from that attempt. Return to the move and try it again.
The saved engine analysis shows a forced checkmate. It is for the side that made this move.
After this move, the saved engine analysis finds a forced checkmate for the other side.
When the saved line ends, the side that made this move holds more material than it started with.
When the saved line ends, the side that made this move holds less material than it started with.
The move is accepted for this exercise. The moves shown give no clear tactical reason.
The move is not accepted for this exercise. The moves shown give no clear tactical reason for that.
A saved answer matches this move. For this exercise, the saved answers set what is accepted.
No saved answer matches this move. A different legal move is not, on that account, bad chess.
Stay with the move a moment. Then go on to the next position.
A good move. The reason belongs with it.
The practice is saved. The review schedule does not change.
Solved. The recall remains marked for relearning.
The position before any of the moves. Everything starts from here.
The next move. Something on the board is different now.
Check. The king is under attack, and that must be answered.
The king leaves check with this move.
The pawn reaches the last rank. It becomes a new piece.
The pawn reaches the last rank and becomes a new piece, and the move gives check.
The pawn is promoted on the last rank. Checkmate. No legal square remains for the king.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and its own king leaves check by the same move.
A piece is taken.
A piece is taken, and the king is in check.
A piece is taken, and it is checkmate. The king cannot escape.
A piece is taken, and with it the king leaves check.
Capturing as it arrives, the pawn reaches the last rank and promotes.
Capturing as it arrives, the pawn promotes on the last rank. The move gives check.
The pawn captures, reaches the last rank and promotes. Checkmate comes with it; the king cannot escape.
The pawn captures and becomes a new piece on the last rank. In the same move, its king leaves check.
The king castles and the rook crosses over. Check follows from the same move.
The king castles and the rook crosses over. Checkmate, softly; the other king is out of escapes.
One piece attacks several targets, then takes one. In this example, the fork also ends with a net material gain.
The piece cannot make that capture. It is pinned to its king, and leaving the line would expose the king.
The piece under attack is pinned to its king. Its escape is narrow: only moves that keep the king unexposed are legal.
The defenders cannot take back. They are pinned to their king, and in the shown line, material is gained.
The pinned piece stays on its line, because leaving would expose its king. Before these moves end, it is captured.
The front piece leaves the line. What stood behind it is captured along that same line.
Check forces the king off the line. Then the same attacker takes the piece that stood behind it.
The only defender goes first. Later in these moves, the piece it guarded is captured too.
The defender is drawn away from its task. The piece it was guarding is then taken.
A blocking piece moves. Along the line it opened, another piece makes the capture.
One piece steps aside, and the piece it was hiding gives check.
Double check. Two pieces attack the king at once.
The moved piece attacks one target and opens a line for another. In this example, the second piece takes its target.
The pawn becomes a new piece. In this example, that side ends with a net material gain.
No one guarded the piece, and it is captured. The capturing side ends this example with a net material gain.
The opponent's previous move released a relative pin on the attacking piece. The target was not moved after that, and in the shown line it is captured.
The other side can play the marked reply. Play it on the board and see what follows.
Before moving, find any piece of yours that could be taken with no useful recapture.
Before a quiet move, check for enemy pieces left without a guard.
Check forcing moves where one piece attacks two valuable targets.
Before a pinned piece moves, see what stands behind it: the king, or something of greater value.
An attack can pass through the first target. Check for a valuable piece standing behind it.
Before a defender is exchanged, see what it protects now.
When a blocking piece moves, lines open behind it. Check where they lead.
Look for one move that makes two threats. Checks and opened lines count.
Before a back-rank defender moves, find the king's escape squares.
Count the moves the pawn needs to promote, and weigh each forcing pawn advance.
Before a defender moves, find every piece it protects. Those are the pieces it would leave behind.
Count what the capture takes, and what the recapture takes back.
Check whether a forcing exchange could pull a defender away from something else it guards.
This exercise is defined by its saved answers. A different legal move may still be sound chess.
These moves show play against strong replies. Not every reply here is forced.
Material changes cover only the shown line, counted from its starting position. The written explanation gives the piece values.
The saved line shows no simple tactical reason. Trace it gently, reply by reply. No positional explanation has been assumed.
This explanation follows the answer policy saved for the exercise. The written notes show its setting.
These are the moves of the opening line you are studying.
That move is in your selected study material.
The answer is among your selected study lines. Play one of those moves.
More than one move from your selected opening lines will count here.
One move from your selected study material belongs here. Recall it.
That move is not among the opening lines you selected. Try again.
That move is not in your selected opening lines. Try again. This saved attempt leaves the changed study's review schedule as it is.
That move is not in your selected opening lines. Try again. This position is retired, and its review schedule does not change.
In mixed Due, moves from this line are accepted. Dedicated practice asks for this line by itself.
Scheduled recalls ask for your selected side's moves. Where active studies share a position, they share one card.
The saved session needs to be reloaded. Then make your next move.
The verified line plays on the board.
This attempt is marked as revealed. Below, the solution can be played through again.
Solved, after a retry. The earlier miss and the finish are both kept.
The full solution, and no wrong move. Cleanly found.
That move is not the solution. The correct moves before it remain saved.
That move is right for this puzzle. Another move remains to be found.
Nothing here needs hurrying. Calculate, then move.
The engine has given me too little to explain this position. The board is still open to you.
The review is paused. Resume it below, or move a piece and explore.
Select a move to review it, or move a piece to explore another path.
A book move. This position has been reached before.
This move is in the book, part of a known opening line.
Book. The move sits inside a recognized opening.
Even here, the book whispers along.
The book knows this one too.
The reply is also book.
The known line goes on.
Still on known ground.
Another known move.
The book has not ended yet.
Again, a book move. Being known does not make a move good.

A forced checkmate was there to play. The human-move model expects this move instead, and the mate goes unplayed.
The human-move model expects this move. The reply is a capture, available at once.
This is a likely move, by the human-move model. It is still weaker than the engine's best, and some of the position's value is given up.
One of their pieces could now reach several targets at once, a fork. The human-move model sees this move as natural. The fork is there regardless.
A front piece now shields another on the same line. The other side can try a skewer. The human-move model finds this move natural.

Only this move kept the position playable; the rest that were checked were losing. The human-move model and the alternatives mark it as a hard find.
The advantage stayed, because of this move alone. The other moves checked were losing, and by the human-move model, this one was difficult to see.
Nothing else in the search held the advantage; each was losing. This one did, and the human-move model and the alternatives place it among the hard finds.
One piece reaches several targets at once, a fork. The human-move model does not expect it. The engine finds it strong.

A pin to the king holds a piece on its line. This is the engine's best move, and few hands would ever reach for it, the human-move model judges.
The move looks ordinary. It takes away a piece's only real defender, and the other side can capture what is left unguarded. The human-move model rates it a natural choice.
A piece loses its only real defender, and the other side can capture it. One searched move kept the position playable instead. The human-move model suggests that defense was hard to find.
The threat came with the opponent's last move. This move, a natural one by the human-move model, does not answer it, and a piece can now be captured.
The opponent's last move set the threat. It stays unanswered, and a piece can be captured. Only one of the moves examined held the position, and the human-move model marks it as difficult to see.
The capture is a natural one, by the human-move model. But the recapture takes a more valuable piece. Count both halves of the exchange.
This capture invites the recapture of a more valuable piece. A different move was the only one checked that kept the position playable, and by the human-move model's estimate, it was hard to see.
One piece reaches several targets: a fork. The human-move model expects the move, and the engine ranks it best.
A fork, one piece reaching more than one target. The human-move model would expect it. Strong. Not the engine's first.

A fork is open to the other side now, one of their pieces reaching several targets. Only one searched move kept the position playable, and it went unplayed. By the human-move model, it was hard to find.
A fork was there in another move. This one is more natural to the human-move model, and the fork stays unplayed.

Two pieces on one line; if the front one moves, the one behind is exposed. A skewer. The human-move model finds it natural, and the engine has it as best.
A skewer lies along this line. The human-move model expects the move; the engine finds it strong, though another move ranks higher.

The target is a defender. Capture it, and its protection goes with it. The human-move model does not expect this move; the engine's verdict is strong.
Capturing the defender leaves what it guarded unprotected. The human-move model expects the move, and it is the engine's best.
A defender is taken, and its protection ends. A natural move, by the human-move model. The engine rates it strong; its first choice lies elsewhere.
A defender can now be captured, and what it guards could be left without protection. The human-move model finds this move ordinary.
The other side can capture a defender now. One move among those examined kept the position playable, and it was not played. It was hard to see, by the human-move model's estimate.
Another move could have captured a defender and removed its protection. The human-move model expects this move instead. The defender is still in place.
The only move examined that held the position captured a defender. That move went unplayed, and by the human-move model, it was hard to see.

A back-rank mating idea, the king hemmed in by its own pieces. The human-move model finds the move natural, and the engine ranks it best.
The king's own pieces block its escape, and a back-rank mating idea follows. It is a likely move, by the human-move model. The engine calls it strong, though not its first choice.
A pawn has a road to the last rank, and promotion is the aim. This is the engine's best, and the human-move model marks it as a move most players walk by unseen.

Promotion is the aim, a pawn moving toward the last rank. The human-move model finds this natural, and the engine puts it first.

One of their pawns now has a way toward the last rank. The human-move model finds this move natural, and it gives the other side a chance to promote.
